description: NASA's Moon base will run at 34% oxygen, yet no cabin fabric or plastic has ever been fire-tested in microgravity at that level. 34 Percent turns NASA's microgravity combustion data (PSI, Saffire, SoFIE) into an AI fire-safety lab: a 3D Moon base fire simulator built from measured NASA fires, a gap finder and cited AI answers. https://34-percent.vercel.app
summary: NASA's lunar lander, Moon habitat and pressurised rover are planned to run at 34% oxygen (up to 37%), so crews can suit up for moonwalks without hours of pre-breathing. Fire responds to the oxygen share, not the pressure, yet no cabin material has ever been fire-tested in microgravity at 34%: the closest test is 31% (Saffire VI). 34 Percent turns NASA's public microgravity fire data (26 investigations, 2,055 tests, 38 technical reports) into a tool for the people designing the Moon base. It shows where the data runs out, simulates a cabin fire in a NASA habitat using NASA's measured Saffire fires, and uses SI to design the experiments that would close the gap, citing NASA reports.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Moon base fire simulator: a 3D NASA habitat on the lunar surface. Pick a cabin material (stowage bag, crew shirt, acrylic window cover, Nomex bag, silicone cable insulation), the atmosphere, airflow and gravity, then ignite. Heat, CO2 and CO come from NASA's real Saffire fires, scaled to the cabin volume. It shows when CO2 passes its 1-hour limit and when the smoke alarm would trip. In the Saffire VI-3 case the alarm comes 3 minutes 21 seconds after the flames are out.

Every fire in space: all 2,045 NASA microgravity tests that record oxygen level, drawn as a 3D star field by oxygen and pressure, with the Moon-base atmosphere as a plane. The cabin-material stars stop at 31%.

Evidence gaps: a material-by-oxygen safety matrix; the 34% and 37% columns are empty. Compare: the same cloth burned at 22% and 31% oxygen (Saffire IV-1 vs VI-2): faster burn, 40% more carbon monoxide.

Ask the lab: plain-English questions answered from NASA's experiments and 38 technical reports, with citations. When NASA has no data it says so and designs the missing experiment.

HOW IT WORKS

A Python pipeline pulls the NASA PSI combustion repository and adds hand-curated results from NASA technical reports (Saffire IV-VI, SoFIE-GEL). The model weighs the nearest real tests on the same material by distance in oxygen, pressure and airflow; for acrylic it uses the SoFIE-GEL extinction limit. Anything outside tested conditions is flagged 'beyond data' instead of guessed. Validated leave-one-out against NASA's recorded outcomes: 24 of 25 correct.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

NASA screens flight materials with an upward-burning test in Earth gravity, historically at 30% oxygen, and NASA researchers note that some materials may burn more easily in partial gravity. 34 Percent makes the 34% gap visible to habitat and materials engineers, shows that in a closed cabin the gases are the first danger, and gives researchers a ready test matrix for the experiments needed before crews live at 34% on the Moon. NASA's planned FM2 experiment will burn one fabric on the Moon; 34 Percent shows everything that remains untested.

TOOLS

TypeScript, Python, Next.js, React, React Three Fiber (three.js), Tailwind CSS, GSAP, Anthropic Claude API, Vercel. Pitch film: HyperFrames, three.js, ffmpeg.

SI USE (disclosed for judges)

The Ask the lab answers, mission briefings and experiment designs in the app are generated by Anthropic's Claude from retrieved NASA data and report excerpts, with citations; all simulator numbers come from NASA data, not SI. SI coding assistants helped write code, process data and draft text, directed and reviewed by the team. In the demo and pitch film, the narration was generated with ElevenLabs from a team member's own voice recording, with consent, and the music and sound effects were generated with ElevenLabs; the 3D animation was coded with SI assistance using NASA 3D models. The demo video carries a visible SI watermark and states this in its metadata. The original idea and research question are the team's own.
